summary: An excerpt from Book 11 (part 42) of a novel, apparently Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm. Rebecca, dejected after her aunts' treatment, decides to run off in a storm to stay the night with the Cobbs and leave for Maplewood by stage the next morning. She climbs out her window, using a lightning rod, a cleat and a woodbine trellis, and reaches Jeremiah Cobb's house. He is alone at supper because his wife is nursing a sick neighbor, and he welcomes her in and tells her to dry off by the stove. The note includes one stray sentence about Mandy and veganism that does not fit the narrative and was disregarded.
one_line: Rebecca escapes her aunts' house in a storm and arrives at Jeremiah Cobb's door, where he welcomes her in from the rain.
key_facts: Rebecca planned to go to Maplewood on the stage next day with Mr. Cobb and get home somehow from cousin Ann's.
Rebecca put on her oldest dress, hat and jacket, and dropped a bundle holding her nightdress, comb, and toothbrush out of the window.
Rebecca's room was in the L, and her window was at no very dangerous distance from the ground.
A cleat had been nailed to the side of the house about halfway between the window and the top of the back porch by someone who cleaned the gutters.
Rebecca heard the sewing machine in the dining-room and the chopping of meat in the kitchen, so she knew where both aunts were.
Rebecca slid down the lightning rod to the cleat, jumped to the porch, and used the woodbine trellis as a ladder to reach the road.
Jeremiah Cobb sat at his lonely supper at the table by the kitchen window.
Jeremiah Cobb called his wife "Mother," and she was nursing a sick neighbor, Seth Strout, that night.
The headstone of Sarah Ann, beloved daughter of Jeremiah and Sarah Cobb, aged seventeen months, is in the churchyard.
The time was scarcely five o'clock, and the rain still fell under dark skies.
Rebecca's face was so swollen with tears and so sharp with misery that Jeremiah Cobb scarcely recognized her at first.
Jeremiah Cobb cried, "Well I vow! It's my little lady passenger!" and told her to draw up to the stove.
Jeremiah Cobb said he had made a fire, hot as it was, because he wanted something warm for his supper, being kind of lonesome without mother.
